= MocKMP
:toc: macro
:toclevels: 2
:idprefix:
:idseparator: -
:icons: font
:source-highlighter: highlight.js

*Compile-time mocks and fakes for Kotlin Multiplatform tests — generated by a KSP processor, not by reflection.*

MocKMP turns a plain interface or abstract class into a mock or a fake for your tests.
You ask for what a test needs with an annotation — `@Mock`, `@Fake`, `@UsesMocks`, `@UsesFakes` — and a
KSP processor generates the implementation, ready to inject.

.MyTest.kt
[source,kotlin]
----
class MyTest : TestsWithMocks() {
    override fun setUpMocks() = mocker.injectMocks(this)

    @Mock lateinit var view: View
    @Fake lateinit var model: Model

    val controller by withMocks { Controller(view = view, firstModel = model) }

    @Test fun controllerTest() {
        every { view.render(isAny()) } returns true
        controller.start()
        verify { view.render(model) }
    }
}
----

No reflection, no dynamic proxies, no "relaxed" mode papering over a call nobody mocked.
An interface, a generated implementation, and a compiler that rejects a mock or a fake for a type
that can't be one.

toc::[]


== Why MocKMP

*Compile-time, not reflection.* A KSP processor generates a real class implementing the interface or
abstract class you asked to mock or fake, so it behaves identically on every target — including the
ones with no runtime reflection at all, like iOS, JS and Wasm.

*Mocking and faking answer different questions.* A ``mock``'s behaviour is defined per test, and every
call on it can be verified; a ``fake``'s data is inert and zero-valued, and nothing about it is
checked. Reach for a fake when a collaborator only needs to *exist*, and a mock when the test needs to
configure or verify it.

*Nothing is generated until you ask for it.* `@UsesMocks` / `@UsesFakes` — or a `@Mock` / `@Fake`
property — requests exactly the types a given test needs, so an interface used across a large
codebase doesn't grow generated code everywhere it's declared, only where it's actually mocked or
faked.

*Injection kills the constructor boilerplate.* Annotate properties `@Mock` or `@Fake` and call
`mocker.injectMocks(this)`; inherited properties are injected too, so a shared base test class works
exactly as if its mocks had been declared locally.

*The `TestsWithMocks` helper collapses the ceremony further.* Inherit it and get a `Mocker`, an
automatic reset before every test, `withMocks` property delegates rebuilt fresh each time, and
`every` / `everySuspending` / `verify` / `verifyWithSuspend` callable without the `mocker.` prefix.

*Constraints read the same in a definition and in a verification.* `isAny`, `isEqual`, `isNotNull`,
`isInstanceOf`, and any custom constraint you write with `isValid`, work identically whether they
appear inside `every` or inside `verify` — one matcher vocabulary, not two.

*Multiplatform, with no platform-specific surprises.* `mockmp-runtime` targets every platform MocKMP
supports and behaves the same on each of them.


== Installation

WARNING: Version 2.0 brings compatibility with Kotlin 2.0, but with breaking changes.
If you're on version 1.17, see the
https://kosi-libs.org/mockmp/2.0/migration/1to2.html[1.x to 2.x migration guide].

WARNING: Version 3.0 brings compatibility with AGP 9, but becomes *incompatible* with AGP 8 or
earlier.
Only update to MocKMP 3.0 if you are also updating to AGP 9 — if you're on version 2.1, see the
https://kosi-libs.org/mockmp/3.0/migration/2to3.html[2.x to 3.x migration guide].

Apply the Gradle plugin to your Kotlin/Multiplatform module, then enable it on the test source sets
you want mocks and fakes generated for:

.build.gradle.kts
[source,kotlin,subs="verbatim,attributes"]
----
plugins {
    kotlin("multiplatform")
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp")                      // <1>
    id("org.kodein.mock.mockmp") version "{version}"    // <2>
}

kotlin {
    // Your Kotlin/Multiplatform configuration
}

mockmp {                                                // <3>
    onTest {
        withHelper()                                    // or withHelper(junit5)
    }
}
----
<1> KSP hosts the MocKMP processor.
<2> The MocKMP Gradle plugin — it wires the runtime and the processor for you, so there is no
    dependency to add by hand.
<3> Configured *after* the `kotlin { }` block, so the plugin can see your targets.
    `withHelper()` also pulls in the `TestsWithMocks` helper class.

The plugin applies just as well to a single-target `kotlin("jvm")` or `kotlin("android")` project.
